content: The Unity for Gallaudet Movement was a protest initiated by students, faculty, alumni of Gallaudet University, and other supporters who opposed the appointment of Dr. Jane Fernandes as the university's ninth president. This movement arose following the announcement of I. King Jordan, the university's previous president, that he would retire at the end of 2006. Jordan, who had been appointed as a result of the Deaf President Now Movement in 1988, saw his successor narrowed down to three candidates. Ultimately, Ronald Stern and Stephen Weiner were eliminated, leaving Fernandes as the chosen candidate. On May 1, 2006, Celia May Baldwin, the chairperson of the Board of Trustees, announced Dr. Jane Fernandes as the next president of Gallaudet University. This announcement was met with significant backlash from the audience, who protested the decision. A few weeks later, Baldwin resigned from her position on the Board of Trustees, citing threats she had received regarding the selection of Fernandes. On September 20, 2006, the Gallaudet Student Congress passed a resolution stating that they did not recognize Jane K. Fernandes as the university's ninth president. Key figures in the protest included Ryan Commerson, LaToya Plummer, Leah Katz-Hernandez, and Delia Lozano-Martinez, who served as spokespersons for the Faculty, Staff, Students, and Alumni (FSSA). Chris Corrigan, referred to as the Mayor of Tent City, played a significant role in organizing rallies. Noah Beckman, the Student Body Government (SBG) president, and Tara Holcomb, the SBG's Director of Ethics and Conduct, emerged as prominent voices for the student body. Former SBG president and alumna Tawny Holmes, along with graduate student Erin Moran, also played critical roles in encouraging students to voice their opposition to Fernandes' appointment. During October, Commerson acted as the democratic leader of the protest, with Holmes and Moran serving as his primary deputies. Alumnus Sean Moore was also actively involved. On October 1, 2006, students attempted to revive Tent City, a symbolic protest site, but encountered issues when campus workers had recently applied a highly concentrated liquid fertilizer called Earth Juice to the area. The administration claimed that the fertilization had been planned months in advance. Despite this, Tent City was reestablished the following day to continue protesting the selection of Fernandes. Eventually, students escalated their actions by seizing and locking down the Hall Memorial Building (HMB), effectively halting classes and pressuring the university administration to negotiate. On October 6, 2006, officers from the Department of Public Safety raided the Hall Memorial Building in an attempt to end the lockdown. Students later alleged that officers had assaulted several of them during the raid. In response, I. King Jordan ordered an independent investigation into the incident. On October 12, 2006, police were called in to arrest the protesting students. On October 13, 2006, known as Black Friday, 133 individuals, including Tim Rarus, one of the leaders of the 1988 Deaf President Now Movement, were arrested at Gallaudet University under orders from I. King Jordan. Before his arrest, Rarus reportedly shouted, I helped put you in office, now you're arresting me. The following day, the number of protesters swelled from 300 to nearly 1,000, with Gallaudet alumni flying in to support the students. Tom Holcomb, a leader among the alumni, had arrived earlier in the week to assist with organizing the protest and establishing a shift system. Bobbie Beth Scoggins, president of the National Association of the Deaf (NAD), cut her vacation short to declare the NAD's support for the students' demands. On October 16, 2006, 168 of the 221 eligible voting faculty members at Gallaudet University attended a faculty meeting, representing 76% of the eligible voting faculty and marking the largest attendance ever recorded. On October 19, 2006, The Washington Post reported that of the 20 trustees on the Board, three of whom were members of Congress, as many as seven did not support Fernandes becoming president. Finally, on October 29, 2006, the Gallaudet Board of Trustees withdrew its appointment of Jane Fernandes as president, without naming an alternative candidate.
